content: Blood plasma is the liquid component of blood in which blood cells are suspended. It constitutes approximately 55% of the total blood volume. Blood plasma can be obtained by centrifuging a tube of fresh blood until the blood cells settle at the bottom, after which the plasma is either poured off or drawn out. A medical procedure known as plasmapheresis involves separating plasma from red blood cells. Blood plasma contains several essential proteins, including fibrinogen (a clotting factor), globulins, and human serum albumin. Occasionally, plasma may harbor viral impurities, which must be removed through viral processing. Plasma is clear and pale yellow in color, primarily composed of water, blood proteins, and inorganic electrolytes. The proteins in plasma are critical for maintaining oncotic pressure, which helps retain plasma within the blood vessels despite their permeability. Plasma also serves as a transport medium for glucose, lipids, amino acids, hormones, metabolic waste products, carbon dioxide (CO2), and oxygen (O2). However, the oxygen transport capacity of plasma is significantly lower than that of hemoglobin in red blood cells, although CO2 levels in plasma can increase under hyperbaric conditions. Plasma also acts as a storage and transport medium for clotting factors. Blood serum, in contrast, is plasma from which clotting factors have been removed, achieved by allowing fresh blood to clot before centrifugation. Fresh frozen plasma (FFP) is derived from a single unit of blood collected from one individual. It is frozen shortly after collection and can be stored for up to one year. FFP retains all the coagulation factors and proteins present in the original blood unit. It is used to treat coagulopathies caused by warfarin overdose, liver disease, or dilutional coagulopathy. If FFP is stored beyond the standard time frame, it is reclassified as frozen plasma, which is similar but has reduced viability of coagulation factors. FFP is also used to treat thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), as platelet transfusion is not a viable treatment for this condition. Dried plasma was developed and first utilized during World War II. Before the United States entered the war, liquid plasma and whole blood were used. A significant project began in August 1940 to collect blood in New York City hospitals for plasma export to Britain. Dr. Charles Drew was appointed as the medical supervisor of the Plasma for Britain project. He played a pivotal role in transforming small-scale test tube methods into the first successful mass production techniques for blood plasma. However, the decision was made to develop dried plasma packages for the armed forces to reduce breakage and simplify transportation, packaging, and storage. The resulting Army-Navy dried plasma package consisted of two tin cans containing 400 cc bottles. One bottle held distilled water sufficient to reconstitute the dried plasma in the other bottle. The plasma could be prepared for use in about three minutes and remained viable for approximately four hours. Following the Plasma for Britain project, Dr. Drew was named director of the Red Cross blood bank and assistant director of the National Research Council, overseeing blood collection for the U.S. Army and Navy. Dr. Drew opposed the military directive requiring blood and plasma to be segregated by the donor's race, arguing that there was no racial difference in human blood and that such a policy would result in unnecessary deaths as soldiers and sailors waited for same-race blood. By the end of the war, the American Red Cross had supplied enough blood for over six million plasma packages, with most surplus plasma returned to the U.S. for civilian use. During the Korean War, serum albumin replaced dried plasma for combat use.
